reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Present as dilated, tortuous, superficial leg veins, often with aching, heaviness, itching, or swelling that worsens with prolonged standing and eases on elevation
Most arise from primary valvular incompetence in the great or small saphenous systems, allowing reflux and venous hypertension
Assessment includes standing inspection and duplex ultrasound to map the sites of reflux and incompetent junctions, which has largely replaced the older tourniquet tests
Chronic venous hypertension produces skin changes: haemosiderin pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, and ultimately venous ulceration around the gaiter area
Conservative measures include graduated compression stockings, weight loss, exercise, and leg elevation
Interventional options include endovenous thermal ablation (laser or radiofrequency), foam sclerotherapy, and conventional surgery (ligation and stripping)
Secondary varicose veins may follow deep vein thrombosis or pelvic outflow obstruction, so a history of DVT and signs of deep venous disease should be sought
Sudden bleeding from a ruptured varicosity is controlled by elevation and direct compression, not by a tourniquet
reference.pathophysiology: Varicose veins develop when incompetent valves in the superficial venous system, or at the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions, permit reflux of blood back down the leg. The resulting venous hypertension dilates and elongates the superficial veins, making them tortuous. Sustained ambulatory venous hypertension is transmitted to the skin microcirculation, causing capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, inflammation, and progressive skin changes that culminate in venous ulceration. Contributing factors include heredity, prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity, and previous deep vein thrombosis, the last causing secondary varicosities through deep venous obstruction or valvular damage.
additionalDifferentials: Deep venous insufficiency or post-thrombotic syndrome
Klippel-Trenaunay and other congenital venous malformations
Arterial disease contributing to leg ulceration
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound to map superficial and deep reflux and identify incompetent junctions and perforators
Ankle-brachial pressure index before compression therapy to exclude significant arterial disease
Assessment for prior deep vein thrombosis and deep venous patency
Photographs or clinical grading (e.g. CEAP classification) to document severity
redFlags: Torrential haemorrhage from a ruptured surface varicosity requiring elevation and direct pressure
Non-healing venous ulcer, especially with atypical features suggesting malignant change (Marjolin's ulcer)
Signs of deep vein thrombosis or coexisting significant arterial disease before compression
Rapidly progressive skin changes or superficial thrombophlebitis extending toward the saphenofemoral junction
reference.prognosis: Symptoms and skin changes usually improve with compression and, where appropriate, ablation or surgery, and venous ulcers can heal with effective compression, but recurrence of varicosities and ulcers is common, particularly with deep venous disease or poor compliance.
pitfalls: Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial disease
Overlooking underlying deep venous disease or previous DVT causing secondary varicosities
Attempting to control variceal bleeding with a tourniquet rather than elevation and compression
Missing malignant change in a chronic non-healing venous ulcer
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Offer conservative management first with graduated compression stockings, leg elevation, regular exercise and weight reduction, particularly where intervention is declined or contraindicated
Confirm adequate arterial supply with the ankle-brachial pressure index before applying compression
Treat truncal saphenous reflux with endovenous thermal ablation by radiofrequency or laser as first-line, reserving ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy or open ligation and stripping as alternatives
Map the sites of superficial and deep reflux with duplex ultrasound to target intervention
Manage skin sequelae of venous hypertension, treating venous eczema with emollients and topical corticosteroids and gaiter-area ulceration with multilayer compression
Refer to vascular services for symptomatic varicosities, progressive skin changes, bleeding varicosities or superficial thrombophlebitis
Maintain compression and surveillance long term to reduce recurrence, especially where deep venous disease coexists
